source: Wellman, Cross & Watson (2001) Meta-analysis of theory-of-mind development: the truth about false belief
finding: Across 178 studies, 3-year-olds were below chance on false belief and 4-year-olds above chance. The pattern held across countries and task variants. Authors read this as conceptual change (theory-theory) rather than task artifact.
numbers: N=178 studies. Age + country + four task factors: multiple R=.74, R2=.55. Primary conditions (362): age alone R2=.39. Below chance at about 41 months and younger, above chance at about 48 months and older.
quote: The findings are inconsistent with early competence proposals that claim developmental changes are due to tasks artifacts
limits: Cannot separate theory change from simulation development; both camps can explain an age curve.
agent_relevance: Treat social inference in a scaffold as a graded skill with task-dependent difficulty, not one on/off ability.

source: Wellman, Cross & Watson (2001) Meta-analysis of theory-of-mind development: the truth about false belief (effect sizes)
finding: Four task features helped even young children: motive to deceive the protagonist, active participation, salience of the real state, and real presence of the protagonist.
numbers: Age effect: odds of a correct answer rise 2.94 times per year (about 1.09 per month). About 50% correct at 44 months; 74.6% at 56 months. Omnibus analysis (453 conditions): R2=.28, age slope .090.
limits: Task factors help but do not remove the developmental trend.
agent_relevance: Prompt framing changes answers a lot in LLMs too. Control task wording when checking social reasoning.

source: Devine & Hughes (2014) Relations between false belief understanding and executive function in early childhood: a meta-analysis
finding: Executive function and false belief are moderately linked. Early EF predicts later false belief but not the reverse. Same link across cultures. Authors favour a hybrid emergence-expression account.
numbers: 102 studies, 9,994 children aged 3-6. Moderate association; similar across cultures; asymmetric over time.
limits: Abstract page only. Correlational. Does not choose between simulation (needs inhibiting own view) and theory (needs selecting a theory).
agent_relevance: Holding one's own knowledge apart from the other's is a cost in mind-reading. A scaffold step may need to make this separation explicit.

source: Milligan, Astington & Dack (2007) Language and theory of mind: meta-analysis of the relation between language ability and false-belief understanding
finding: Language ability predicts false belief with a moderate to large effect that survives age control. Earlier language predicts later false belief more strongly than the reverse. Receptive vocabulary is weaker than general language.
numbers: 104 studies, N=8,891, children under 7. No significant difference among false-belief task types.
limits: Abstract page only. Fits a role for language and concepts (theory side) but does not rule out simulation.
agent_relevance: Language-based representations of others' views may carry much of mental-state reasoning in language models.

source: Hofmann et al. (2016) Training children's theory-of-mind: a meta-analysis of controlled studies
finding: Training children on mental states works. Longer sessions and active-control designs gave larger gains.
numbers: 32 papers, 45 studies, 1,529 children (mean age 63 months, SD 28.7). Hedges g=0.75, 95% CI 0.60-0.89, p<.001.
limits: Abstract page read and cut off early. Transfer to everyday behaviour not shown here. Does not separate simulation-type from theory-type training.
agent_relevance: Explicit instruction on mental-state concepts helps. Supports adding explicit concept rules to a scaffold, not only perspective-taking prompts.

source: Schuwerk, Priewasser, Sodian & Perner (2018) The robustness and generalizability of findings on spontaneous false belief sensitivity: a replication attempt
finding: Anticipatory-looking false-belief effect failed to replicate in toddlers and in a preregistered 25-month-old sample, but replicated in adults. Many children did not anticipate during familiarization, causing heavy exclusions.
numbers: Exp 1: 2-3 year olds N=48 failed. Preregistered Exp 2: 25-month-olds N=78 failed; adults N=115 succeeded.
limits: Failure to replicate does not prove no competence; the task may be unreliable. Authors say exclusions limit interpretability.
agent_relevance: Early implicit mind-reading evidence is weak. Do not design from claims that simple perspective tracking is innate and automatic.

source: Kampis, Karman, Csibra, Southgate & Hernik (2021) A two-lab direct replication attempt of Southgate, Senju and Csibra (2007)
finding: Preregistered replication including two original authors found no evidence of false-belief action anticipation in 2-year-olds. Only about half of infants looked to the target location even without a belief requirement.
numbers: N=160 infants aged 24-26 months, two labs, original stimuli. About half anticipated on true-belief trials and a similar share on false-belief trials.
limits: Authors say results neither support nor deny infant ToM; the paradigm cannot assess it.
agent_relevance: Large careful replications change the picture. Weight preregistered large-sample evidence above famous single studies.

source: Epley, Keysar, Van Boven & Gilovich (2004) Perspective taking as egocentric anchoring and adjustment
finding: People take another's view by starting from their own and adjusting, usually too little. This is a simulation-style process with a known bias. Time pressure raises egocentric bias; accuracy incentives lower it. People stop adjusting once an estimate seems plausible.
numbers: Five studies. Study 2: slower to say another's perception differs; bias up under time pressure. Study 3: bias down with accuracy incentives. Study 5: adjustment stops at plausibility.
limits: Abstract page only; sample sizes not read. Anchor-and-adjust is one simulation variant, not the only one.
agent_relevance: A simulate-the-other step should force several adjustment passes and reward accuracy; one-pass simulation under-adjusts.

source: Van Overwalle & Baetens (2009) Understanding others' actions and goals by mirror and mentalizing systems: a meta-analysis
finding: Over 200 fMRI studies: the mirror system engages for body-part action; the mentalizing system (TPJ, mPFC, precuneus) engages for abstract cues like stories and shapes. The two are rarely active together, so they look complementary, not one built on the other.
numbers: More than 200 fMRI studies. TPJ overlap between social and non-social orienting tasks.
limits: Abstract page only. Neuroimaging overlap is weak evidence for simulation. Suggests a hybrid.
agent_relevance: Match method to input: concrete observed actions can use simulation-style matching; abstract verbal scenarios call for rule-based inference.

source: Wilf, Lee, Liang & Morency (2024) Think Twice: Perspective-Taking Improves Large Language Models' Theory-of-Mind Capabilities (SimToM)
finding: SimToM is a two-stage simulation-theory prompt: first keep only what the character knows, then answer. It beat zero-shot and chain-of-thought on false-belief items for weaker models, but not for GPT-4 on BigToM.
numbers: BigToM false belief, GPT-3.5-Turbo: +29.5 points over zero-shot, +14.2 over CoT. ToMI false belief: +16, +19, +47 points over CoT for Llama2-7b, Llama2-13b, GPT-3.5. GPT-4 on BigToM: slight decrease. On GPT-3.5 BigToM false belief, SC-CoT 33.5 vs SimToM 81.0.
limits: Synthetic templated benchmarks; BigToM was generated with GPT-4. Gains shrink on true-belief controls and strong models.
agent_relevance: Cheap usable operator: filter context to what the other party knows, then answer. Useful for weaker models; check it does not hurt strong ones.

source: Wilf et al. (2024) SimToM ablations
finding: Splitting the filter step from the answer step into two prompts matters. Hand-written (oracle) perspective filters give far more than model-made ones, so the bottleneck is deciding who knows what.
numbers: GPT-3.5. Oracle perspectives: ToMI false belief 81.0 -> 96; BigToM false belief 70.5 -> 96.0. Multi-step rationale variant: BigToM false belief 58.75 (-22.25 vs SimToM). Domain-specific variant: 31.75 (-49.25).
limits: One model for ablations. The single-prompt row was not legible in the extracted table.
agent_relevance: Perspective-filter quality is the limit. Check the filter step separately before the answer step.

source: Aoki & Kawahara (2025) Testing Simulation Theory in LLMs' Theory of Mind
finding: First direct test of simulation theory inside LLMs. A linear map from the model's representation of a false-belief story to its representation of the same story told in first person was learned; steering along it flipped answers from false-belief to true-belief more than a control did. Authors conclude simulation theory may partially explain LLM ToM.
numbers: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, 200 BigToM false-belief items; 198 and 196 answered correctly and kept; 8:2 train/test split. Net intervention effect rises in later layers (heatmap values up to about 0.2) against an ideal of 1.
limits: Small effect; linear map only; two models; authors say it cannot fully account for the mechanism. Does not show simulation beats theory.
agent_relevance: First-person re-description is a legitimate operation: restate the scenario from the other's point of view before answering.

source: Zhu, Zhang & Wang (2024) Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
finding: Belief status of self and other agents can be decoded linearly from activations, and steering these directions changes ToM answers a lot.
numbers: BigToM, Mistral-7B, steering along the oracle-belief direction (+TpFo): forward belief false-belief 0.98, both 0.97; forward action false-belief 0.81, both 0.79; backward belief barely moved (0.53, 0.40). GPT-4 forward belief both 0.81.
limits: Table row labels were misaligned in extraction, so assignment to the steered Mistral row is inferred. One small model. A decodable representation does not show use of simulation.
agent_relevance: Separate self and other belief representations exist; both accounts can use them.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Sensitivity Meets Sparsity: extremely sparse parameter patterns and theory of mind in LLMs
finding: Perturbing about 0.001% of ToM-sensitive parameters sharply lowers ToM performance and also hurts contextual localization and language understanding. The sensitive parameters link to rotary positional encoding.
numbers: Perturbation of 0.001% of parameters. Accuracy numbers not extracted.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read. Fits neither account directly.
agent_relevance: Social reasoning in LLMs may depend on general context tracking, so context management is a first-order lever.

source: Kosinski (2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks (PNAS)
finding: Eleven LLMs on 40 bespoke false-belief tasks with true-belief controls. Newer models solve most; older models none. Claim of emergent ToM-like ability.
numbers: A task needs all 8 scenarios correct. Older models 0 tasks; GPT-3 davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5-turbo 20%; ChatGPT-4 (June 2023) 75%, matching 6-year-old children from past studies.
quote: ChatGPT-4 (from June 2023) solved 75% of the tasks, matching the performance of 6-y-old children
limits: Contested by Ullman 2023, Shapira 2023, Hu 2025. Contamination not excluded.
agent_relevance: Headline success on classic tasks is not enough; test the scaffold on perturbed variants.

source: Ullman (2023) Large Language Models Fail on Trivial Alterations to Theory-of-Mind Tasks
finding: Small changes that keep the logic, such as a transparent container or a protagonist who cannot read the label, reverse GPT-3.5's earlier successes. Argues for a skeptical default and that outlying failures outweigh average success.
numbers: GPT-3.5 gave 98% basket probability on the original transfer task, then failed all listed variations. No sample-size table read.
limits: Tested GPT-3.5 only. Later models and cueing prompts may do better (see SimpleToM).
agent_relevance: Treat scaffold gains on classic tasks as unproven until they survive perturbation sets.

source: Shapira et al. (2023) Clever Hans or Neural Theory of Mind? Stress Testing Social Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Six tasks. LLMs show some ToM-like behaviour, but it is far from robust and fails on adversarial examples, suggesting shallow heuristics.
numbers: In the adversarial false-belief set GPT-4 reached 97% on original items and 83.3% on a second category; for 'transparent access' accuracy fell from 66.7% (davinci-002) to 0% (GPT-4).
limits: Numbers read from a garbled extraction; verify against the tables before quoting.
agent_relevance: Adversarial testing of the scaffold; prior that fluent social answers are shortcut-driven.

source: Gu et al. (2026) SimpleToM: Exposing the Gap Between Explicit ToM Inference and Implicit ToM Application in LLMs (ICLR 2026)
finding: Models infer who knows what almost perfectly, but fail to use it when predicting what the person will do or judging whether the action was reasonable. A short reminder of the awareness question closes much of the gap for behavior prediction.
numbers: Mental-state accuracy above 95% for strong models. Behavior prediction: GPT-3.5 7.6%; GPT-4o 49.5%; Llama-3.1-405B 58.3%. Judgment 10% to 24.9% for strong models; best, DeepSeek-R1, 65.8%. With the awareness reminder: Llama-405B 58.3 -> 89.5, GPT-4o 49.5 -> 82.8, Claude-3.5-Sonnet about 96.9; judgment Claude 24.9 -> 84.1. Custom CoT 87.4% vs generic CoT 62.8% overall.
limits: Gains are fragile: generic system prompts changed accuracy only -2.2 to +6.3 points. Not a direct simulation vs theory test.
agent_relevance: After inferring a mental state, add a step that applies it to the prediction. Do not assume inference carries through.

source: Jin et al. (2024) MMToM-QA: Multimodal Theory of Mind Question Answering (BIP-ALM)
finding: Theory-based Bayesian inverse planning with language models (BIP-ALM) beat GPT-4V and GPT-4 on belief and goal inference. A theory-like explicit model beat prompting. Humans scored 93%.
numbers: Multimodal overall: humans 93.0; GPT-4V 44.0; BIP-ALM with LLaMA 2 76.7, with GPT-J 75.3. Text-only overall: humans 82.5; GPT-4 48.0; GPT-3.5 38.3; BIP-ALM with GPT-J 71.7. False-belief type 1.2: GPT-4 12.0, GPT-4V 13.0.
limits: Synthetic household environments with a fixed action model. Few-shot and CoT did not consistently help baselines.
agent_relevance: Strong case for an explicit causal model of beliefs and desires over pure prompting. Candidate for a structured operator.

source: Jin et al. (2024) MMToM-QA: SimToM and SymbolicToM baselines
finding: On a harder benchmark the simulation-style SimToM prompt gave only a small gain over plain GPT-4; the belief-tracking SymbolicToM gave more.
numbers: Text-only overall: GPT-4 48.0; SimToM with GPT-4 52.5; SymbolicToM with GPT-4 63.0. False-belief type 1.2: GPT-4 12.0; SimToM 15.0; SymbolicToM 61.0. Goal type 2.3: SymbolicToM 0.0, SimToM 2.7.
limits: One benchmark.
agent_relevance: Perspective filtering alone does not fix false-belief inference on harder tasks; add belief tracking.

source: Street et al. (2024) LLMs achieve adult human performance on higher-order theory of mind tasks
finding: On a newly gathered adult benchmark, GPT-4 and Flan-PaLM reach adult or near-adult level on higher-order ToM; GPT-4 exceeds adults at 6th order.
numbers: Order 2: humans 96%, GPT-4 100%, Flan-PaLM 100%, GPT-3.5 54%. Order 4: humans 82%, GPT-4 95%, Flan-PaLM 95%. Order 3 humans 93%. Statistics N=112 statements.
limits: True/false text statements. Authors say size and fine-tuning both matter. Contamination possible.
agent_relevance: Nesting depth is not the weak point; application and robustness are.

source: Muchovej, Royka, Lee & Jara-Ettinger (2025) GPT-4o Lacks Core Features of Theory of Mind
finding: Tests whether GPT-4o has a theory-like model: coherent, abstract, consistent. Action predictions match a human-like belief-desire-cost model in one domain, but transfer between logically matched domains is weak and predictions and inferences disagree.
numbers: ContainerWorld: highest agreement with HumanToM model. Cross-domain correlation of inferred mental states: beliefs rho=.78 (CI .68-.85); desires rho=.39 (CI .2-.57); costs rho=.18 (CI .09-.27). Validity agreement 77.55 to 88.89%, below ceiling.
quote: social proficiency exhibited by LLMs is not the result of an abstract or consistent ToM
limits: One model (GPT-4o). Authors admit larger models might pass. Tests the theory-theory idea of a causal model, not simulation.
agent_relevance: Theory-theory gives concrete tests (coherence, abstractness, consistency) that a scaffold can be checked against.

source: Hu, Sosa & Ullman (2025) Re-evaluating Theory of Mind evaluation in large language models
finding: Names two meanings of ToM: matching behaviour, or matching the computation. Lists theory inversion (including Bayesian inverse planning), simulation through one's own decision process, and bottom-up feature mapping as rival computations. Argues mixed LLM results come from this unclear target.
numbers: Position paper; no new experiment. Cites Kosinski 2024 (GPT-4 solved 75% of tasks).
limits: No new data. Comparing distributed network activity to symbolic mind models is called unresolved.
agent_relevance: Pick the target before measuring: behaviour match or algorithm match. Tests for the agent should state which.

source: Riemer et al. (2025) Position: Theory of Mind Benchmarks are Broken for Large Language Models
finding: Argues LLM ToM benchmarks copied from human psychology are static and cannot test adaptation to a new partner. Proposes a functional metric based on regret against a partner's policy. Discusses simulation theory as an alternative to theory-style models.
numbers: Llama-3 70B Instruct and Mistral Large 2 tested in repeated games (rock-paper-scissors, iterated prisoner's dilemma and others); literal vs functional ToM reported per game. Table values not extracted.
limits: Numbers not captured; the position is the main finding.
agent_relevance: Test the scaffold on adapting to a new partner over repeated turns, not one-shot questions.

source: Lombardi & Lenci (2025) Doing Things with Words: Rethinking Theory of Mind Simulation in Large Language Models
finding: In the Concordia agent-based simulation, GPT-4 often fails to choose actions from attributed beliefs and fails to make coherent causal effects of actions. Authors say ToM-like ability may be shallow statistical association.
numbers: 200 simulations in 5 tasks built from false-belief patterns. Detailed rates not extracted.
limits: Abstract and method skimmed. 'Simulation' here means agent-based modelling, not simulation theory of mind-reading.
agent_relevance: Action-based test: check the chosen action, not just the stated belief.

source: Babarczy, Lukacs, Vedres & Bujka (2026) Do Large Language Models Possess a Theory of Mind? A Comparative Evaluation Using the Strange Stories Paradigm
finding: Compares LLMs with the Strange Stories paradigm used in developmental and clinical work.
numbers: Not extracted this session.
limits: Only the title and opening were read.
agent_relevance: Not evaluated in detail.

source: Scholl & Leslie (2001) Minds, modules, and meta-analysis
finding: Reply in the same issue as Wellman et al.: the meta-analysis pattern is compatible with early-competence accounts, so the age trend does not choose between camps. Taken from a web search summary, not read.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not opened; the link given is the Wellman PubMed page.
agent_relevance: Developmental curves alone do not discriminate; use process evidence.

source: Kulke, Reiss, Krist & Rakoczy (2018) How robust are anticipatory looking measures of Theory of Mind? Replication attempts across the life span
finding: Preregistered attempt to replicate four influential anticipatory-looking ToM tasks. Search summary: such findings seem less reliable and valid than assumed. Not read.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not opened; search snippet only.
agent_relevance: More support for caution with implicit ToM paradigms.
